```text
1	---
2	name: dev-cli
3	description: 'Manage repositories and work-in-progress with the dev CLI: bootstrap existing machines, organise repos without destructive moves, own worktree lifecycle and provisioning, track HOT/WARM/COLD tasks, navigate via TUI, and bridge gh/glab/herdr/tmux. Use when starting, parking or resuming work; scanning or organising repos; choosing a worktree mechanism; fixing worktree setup; or cleaning stale branches, checkouts and sessions.'
4	---
5	
6	# dev-cli
7	
8	The `dev` command is a thin glue layer over git, worktrees, forges and agent
9	runtimes. It exists to stop four different things collapsing into one:
10	
11	```
12	git remote      durable code state, the source of truth
13	git worktree    a disposable local checkout
14	herdr / tmux    a per-host live runtime
15	dev             human intent: what am I working on, and what is next
16	```
17	
18	Everything derivable from git or the runtime is derived live. `dev` persists
19	only what git cannot answer — a task's **state**, **owner** and **next
20	action** — in one TOML file per task under `$XDG_DATA_HOME/dev/tasks/`.
21	
22	**The problem it solves:** when a terminal multiplexer's sidebar is the only
23	record of what you are working on, nothing can ever be closed. `dev` gives that
24	record a home outside the runtime, so closing a session stops meaning
25	abandoning a task.
26	
27	## Check it is there first
28	
29	`dev` is not installed everywhere. Before using it:
30	
31	```bash
32	command -v dev || echo "not installed"
33	dev doctor          # what works on this machine, and what degrades
34	```
35	
36	Only **git** is required. `herdr`, `tmux`, `gh` and `glab` each enable more and
37	degrade cleanly when absent — never make a step hard-depend on one.
38	
39	## Worktree ownership — read this before creating any worktree
40	
41	There are three mechanisms that create git worktrees, and picking the wrong one
42	is the most common source of confusion. The rule:
43	
44	| Kind of worktree | Owner | Where | Lifetime |
45	|---|---|---|---|
46	| Feature, fix, experiment, cross-machine handoff — anything you might return to | **`dev`** | `paths.worktree_path`, default `~/Worktrees/<repo>/<branch-slug>` | until `dev done` or `dev sweep` |
47	| Turn-scoped subagent isolation (`isolation: worktree`, `/batch`, `EnterWorktree`) | **Claude Code** | `.claude/worktrees/` (keep gitignored) | dies with the turn |
48	| `herdr worktree create` | **not used** — `dev` runs `git worktree add` itself, then `herdr worktree open --path …` | — | — |
49	
50	**Rule of thumb: might a human come back to it tomorrow → `dev`. Does it die
51	with this agent turn → Claude Code native.**
52	
53	Why `dev` does not delegate to `herdr worktree create`: the path policy has to
54	hold on machines where herdr is not installed. `dev` creates the checkout with
55	plain git and asks herdr only to *open* it — which still makes it appear in the
56	sidebar grouped under its parent repo with its own branch and ahead/behind row.
57	
58	Never nest a `dev` worktree inside a repository. A checkout inside another
59	checkout makes every indexer, file watcher and `rg` run see a second copy of
60	the tree. `dev` refuses to do it.
61	
62	Full detail: `references/worktree-ownership.md`.
63	
64	## The task lifecycle
65	
66	| State | Git | Runtime | Meaning |
67	|---|---|---|---|
68	| 🔥 `hot` | worktree + branch | session open | working on it now |
69	| 🌤 `warm` | worktree + branch kept | session **closed** | back within days |
70	| ❄️ `cold` | committed and pushed; worktree removed | nothing | paused, reconstructible anywhere |
71	| ✅ `done` | merged | nothing | entry survives until swept |
72	
73	```bash
74	dev repo open api                                  # ad hoc; no task/worktree
75	dev start api --task "typo" --direct                # track current/main directly
76	dev start api --task "small" --branch-only --base main
77	dev start api --task "token refresh" --base main   # isolated worktree → hot
78	dev park --next "add the regression test" --wip    # → warm, session closed
79	dev park --cold --push                             # → cold, worktree removed
80	dev resume "token refresh"                         # → hot, rebuilt if needed
81	dev done --ff                                      # → done, integrated
82	```
83	
84	**Parking is the move that matters.** `dev park --next "…"` is what makes it
85	safe to close a session, and the `--next` text is what makes resuming cheap.
86	Always suggest a `--next` when parking.
87	
88	Full detail: `references/task-lifecycle.md`.
89	
90	## Pick the task's checkout mode
91	
92	A task does not imply a worktree. Use the lightest explicit boundary:
93	
94	- `dev repo open <repo>` / REPOS Enter — ad-hoc open, no task at all.
95	- `dev start … --direct` / REPOS `d` — track current branch (usually main),
96	  create no branch/worktree. HOT ↔ WARM only; `dev done` needs no merge mode.
97	- `dev start … --branch-only` — create and switch a branch in the canonical
98	  checkout. No concurrent branch there.
99	- `dev start …` / REPOS `s` — default isolated branch + worktree. Use once work
100	  may be interrupted, experimental, or parallel.
101	
102	Do not create isolation before it has a job, but do not carry dirty main changes
103	into a parallel task implicitly either: a worktree starts from committed HEAD.
104	Checkpoint first when the new task depends on that work.
105	
106	## Everyday commands
107	
108	```bash
109	dev                        # interactive dashboard (plain listing when piped)
110	dev edit                   # open the effective config; generate it first if absent
111	dev ls                     # what am I working on, everywhere
112	dev ls --json              # stable machine-readable form (also over ssh)
113	dev status                 # what is this directory: repo, branch, task, session
114	dev sweep                  # what has gone stale or drifted, and what to do
115	dev sweep --apply          # act on it, confirming each change
116	
117	dev wt create feat/auth --base main    # worktree at the configured path
118	dev wt list                            # every worktree of this repo
119	dev wt plan                            # what a new worktree would be set up with
120	dev wt plan --write                    # seed a committed .dev.toml from it
121	dev wt rm feat/auth                    # remove the checkout; the branch stays
122	
123	dev repo list              # every repo under the scan roots
124	dev repo clone owner/name  # clone into the right place, via gh or glab
125	dev repo sync --all        # fetch + prune, and report what moved
126	dev repo remote [query]     # search authenticated gh + glab repositories
127	dev bootstrap ~/code       # recursively inventory an existing machine
128	dev bootstrap ~/code --index ~/Projects   # plan a non-destructive symlink catalog
129	dev gitignore              # .gitignore from GitHub templates + the common bits
130	dev adopt                  # import existing worktrees/sessions/branches as tasks
131	
132	dev try redis-streams      # dated scratch directory for an experiment
133	dev graduate redis-streams --category Infra   # promote it into a real project
134	
135	dev stats --heatmap        # where the time actually went
136	dev stats backfill --repo api  # seed one repo; TUI H then b does this in place
137	dev stats path             # durable XDG data, not cache
138	dev cache list             # regenerable forge/gitignore caches
139	dev help worktrees         # quick-reference pages
140	```
141	
142	Complete generated reference: `references/commands.md`.
143	
144	## Bootstrapping and adopting an existing machine
145	
146	Read `references/bootstrap.md` before recursively scanning paths, creating a
147	symlink index, moving physical repositories, or generating layout config. Move
148	is destructive and must follow its report → review → apply procedure.
149	
150	There is nothing to migrate for ordinary use. `dev` discovers repositories through
151	`paths.scan_roots` and never moves, renames or deletes anything.
152	
153	```bash
154	dev config init     # detects this machine's roots; every value stays editable
155	dev adopt           # report existing worktrees, sessions and unmerged branches
156	dev adopt --apply   # record them as tasks (nothing on disk changes)
157	```
158	
159	Do not assume the user's layout is `~/Documents/Program`. Run `dev config show`
160	or `dev repo list` to see what this machine is actually configured for.
161	
162	## Dashboard and forge inventory
163	
164	The TUI has TASKS, REPOS and REMOTE views, switched with tab or vim-style h/l.
165	REMOTE queries authenticated `gh` and `glab` lazily, uses a short-lived private
166	cache, and `/` filters provider, owner/name and description. Enter opens a local
167	clone; `c` confirms before cloning an absent remote. Use `dev repo remote
168	[query] --json` for the non-interactive form; `--cached` avoids a network query.
169	
170	REPOS has explicit LIVE and LATEST columns: latest is the newest dirty-file
171	mtime, commit, or task update. Detail shows the Herdr/tmux handle and agent
172	status. `[tui.repos]` chooses columns and default sort; `O` cycles sort and `R`
173	reverses it.
174	
175	`H` opens the selected repo's heatmap. On an empty panel, `b` backfills only
176	that repo and redraws; `r` rereads existing stats. Stats live in
177	`$XDG_DATA_HOME/dev/stats.db` and are durable observations, not cache — use
178	`dev stats clear` with an explicit scope. `dev cache clear` only removes
179	regenerable forge/gitignore data under `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/dev`.
180	
181	`e` edits config and returning live-reloads data/tool bindings; `r` reloads
182	explicitly. Runtime
183	backend changes require restarting the TUI.
184	
185	External tools are explicit `[[tui.tools]]` config. Run `dev tui tools` before
186	recommending a binding; it shows the exact command and whether it is available.
187	Commands run through `$SHELL` in the selected checkout. For an alias/function
188	that exists only in shell rc, set `interactive = true`; dev uses `$SHELL -lic`
189	and evaluates the command after rc loading. Prefer an executable on PATH when
190	the binding should be portable across machines.
191	
192	## Editing configuration
193	
194	Use `dev edit` (or `dev config edit`) rather than guessing the XDG path. It
195	opens the file selected by `--config`, generating the machine-detected starter
196	when absent, and resolves `--editor` → `$VISUAL` → `$EDITOR` → nvim/vim/vi.
197	
198	## Rules for agents
199	
200	1. **Do not equate task with worktree.** Ad-hoc opening needs no task; `--direct`
201	   tracks current/main; `--branch-only` is lightweight isolation; default
202	   worktree is for interruption/experimentation/parallelism.
203	
204	2. **Always pass `--base` for branch/worktree tasks.** Without it a new branch starts from the current
205	   HEAD, so starting a task while standing on `feature/A` silently builds on
206	   `feature/A`. This is the single most common way to produce a confusing
207	   history unattended.
208	
209	3. **Never `--force` a worktree removal on your own.** `dev wt rm` refuses a
210	   checkout with uncommitted changes; that refusal is the feature. Ask the
211	   user before overriding it.
212	
213	4. **Report drift, do not fix it silently.** `dev sweep` without `--apply`
214	   changes nothing. Show the user its output rather than running `--apply --yes`
215	   for them.
216	
217	5. **Prefer a checkpoint commit over `git stash`.** A stash is invisible in the
218	   log, easy to forget, and cannot be pushed — so it can never reach another
219	   machine. `dev park --wip` makes a `wip:` commit instead.
220	
221	6. **One writer per branch at a time.** `dev resume` refuses a task owned by
222	   another host without `--force`. Before overriding, confirm that machine has
223	   pushed.
224	
225	7. **Check `dev wt plan` before blaming a worktree.** A worktree that comes up
226	   broken is nearly always a provisioning gap, not a git problem. The plan
227	   shows the detected project types, which tools are missing, and exactly what
228	   would be copied or run. Dependencies arrive by a per-ecosystem strategy —
229	   `reinstall` (default), `copy`, `link` or `skip` — and dev refuses an unsound
230	   one rather than producing a broken checkout: a virtualenv cannot be copied,
231	   because it bakes its own absolute path into `pyvenv.cfg`.
232	
233	8. **Do not create a worktree per agent.** Worktrees isolate *change streams*;
234	   panes isolate *agents*. Several agents working on disjoint files of one
235	   feature belong in one checkout.
236	
237	9. **Prefer `dev bootstrap --index` over `--move`.** If the problem is
238	   navigation, a symlink catalog solves it without changing the authoritative
239	   paths. For a physical move, never add `--apply --yes` on the user's behalf;
240	   blocked rows are preconditions to resolve, not checks to bypass.
241	
242	10. **`dev adopt` without `--apply` changes nothing.** Show the user its report
243	   rather than applying it for them — which branches count as work in flight is
244	   their judgement, not yours.
245	
246	11. **Do not call stats.db a cache.** Session/WakaTime observations may not be
247	   reconstructible. Use `dev stats clear --repo/--source/--all`; use
248	   `dev cache clear` only for remote/gitignore caches.
249	
250	12. **Read Git state as counts, not a dirty boolean.** `⇡`/`⇣` are upstream
251	   divergence; `=` conflicts, `+` staged, `!` unstaged, `?` untracked. Use
252	   `dev status` or JSON for the unique-path and type breakdown before cleanup.
253	
254	13. **Commit messages stay English** and follow Conventional Commits, even when
255	   the conversation is in another language — see the companion `git-workflow`
256	   skill, which owns commit conventions, SemVer and branch naming. This skill
257	   does not duplicate them.
258	
259	## When to use this skill
260	
261	- "What am I working on?" / "我在做什麼" / too many terminal workspaces open.
262	- Starting, parking or resuming a piece of work.
263	- "Where should this worktree go?" / "should I use `claude --worktree` or herdr?"
264	- A new worktree is missing `node_modules`, `.venv` or `.env`.
265	- Cleaning up stale branches, worktrees and sessions.
266	- Cloning, creating or auditing repositories across a machine.
267	- Promoting an experiment into a real project.
268	- "Which repo do I spend my time in?"
269	- Setting up a `.gitignore`, or a harness worktree showing as untracked.
270	- Adopting a machine that already has repos, worktrees and sessions.
271	- Recursively scanning, indexing, or physically reorganising existing repos.
272	- Configuring a flat repo/worktree layout or generating config for one.
273	
274	## When NOT to use it
275	
276	- **Commit messages, SemVer, branch naming, PR-vs-main tiering** — that is the
277	  `git-workflow` skill. This one links to it rather than restating it.
278	- **Driving herdr panes and agents directly** — that is the `herdr` skill.
279	- A single `git add` + `git commit` needs no tooling at all.
280	
281	## Reference files
282	
283	- `references/bootstrap.md` — read before scanning or organising an existing
284	  machine; includes the non-destructive index default and move safety gates.
285	- `references/worktree-ownership.md` — who owns which worktree, and how a
286	  worktree gets a working environment. Read before creating one.
287	- `references/task-lifecycle.md` — HOT/WARM/COLD/DONE, when to park, and how
288	  work moves between machines.
289	- `references/runtime-herdr.md` — how `dev` and herdr divide responsibility,
290	  and the sidebar configuration that makes task state visible.
291	- `references/commands.md` — the full command reference, generated from the
292	  binary by `dev skill sync` so it cannot drift.
293	
294	## Gotchas
295	
296	- **`dev` is a shell function, not just a binary.** Commands that move you into
297	  a checkout print a `cd` directive for the wrapper installed by
298	  `eval "$(dev shell-init zsh)"`. Without it they print a path and do not move
299	  you — that is not a bug.
300	- **A worktree is a clean checkout.** It has no `node_modules`, no `.venv` and
301	  none of the gitignored env files. `dev` provisions it; `--no-provision`
302	  skips that and leaves you to it.
303	- **Only gitignored files are copied into a worktree.** Listing a *tracked*
304	  file in `worktree.include` does nothing, because git already put it there on
305	  the correct branch — and copying it would overwrite that version.
306	- **Removing a worktree never deletes the branch.** Those are separate
307	  decisions; conflating them is how work gets lost.
308	- **`dev done` defaults to reporting.** With neither `--ff` nor `--pr` it
309	  explains the options and changes nothing.
310	- **The stats sampler must be scheduled.** `dev stats` is empty until
311	  `dev stats backfill` runs once and `dev stats sample` runs periodically.
312
```

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# End-to-end smoke test: drives the real binary through a full task lifecycle
3	# in a throwaway HOME, with the runtime backend pinned to "none" so no
4	# multiplexer is touched.
5	set -euo pipefail
6	
7	ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"
8	BIN="${BIN:-$ROOT/dev}"
9	
10	# Always rebuild. The Go build cache makes this nearly free, and testing a
11	# stale binary against fresh assertions is worse than not testing at all.
12	echo "building $BIN"
13	(cd "$ROOT" && go build -o "$BIN" ./cmd/dev)
14	
15	SANDBOX="$(mktemp -d)"
16	trap 'rm -rf "$SANDBOX"' EXIT
17	
18	export HOME="$SANDBOX/home"
19	export XDG_DATA_HOME="$HOME/.local/share"
20	export XDG_CONFIG_HOME="$HOME/.config"
21	mkdir -p "$HOME/Program"
22	
23	# A local "remote" so the push and cold-park paths are exercised for real.
24	git init --bare --quiet --initial-branch=main "$SANDBOX/origin.git"
25	
26	cat > "$SANDBOX/config.toml" <<CONFIG
27	[paths]
28	scan_roots    = ["$HOME/Program"]
29	project_root  = "$HOME/Program"
30	tries_root    = "$HOME/tries"
31	worktree_root = "$HOME/Worktrees"
32	state_dir     = "$HOME/state"
33	
34	[runtime]
35	backend = "none"
36	
37	[worktree]
38	include     = [".env"]
39	post_create = []
40	CONFIG
41	
42	dev() { "$BIN" --config "$SANDBOX/config.toml" "$@"; }
43	
44	step() { printf '\n\033[1m▸ %s\033[0m\n' "$1"; }
45	fail() { printf '\033[31m✗ %s\033[0m\n' "$1" >&2; exit 1; }
46	ok()   { printf '  \033[32m✓\033[0m %s\n' "$1"; }
47	
48	step "doctor"
49	dev doctor
50	
51	step "create a repo with a gitignored env file"
52	REPO="$HOME/Program/demo"
53	git init --quiet --initial-branch=main "$REPO"
54	git -C "$REPO" config user.email dev@example.test
55	git -C "$REPO" config user.name  "dev e2e"
56	printf '# demo\n'  > "$REPO/README.md"
57	printf '.env\n'    > "$REPO/.gitignore"
58	printf 'TOKEN=x\n' > "$REPO/.env"
59	git -C "$REPO" add README.md .gitignore
60	git -C "$REPO" commit --quiet -m "chore: initial commit"
61	git -C "$REPO" remote add origin "$SANDBOX/origin.git"
62	git -C "$REPO" push --quiet -u origin main
63	ok "demo repo created and pushed"
64	
65	step "repo list"
66	dev repo list | grep -q demo || fail "demo not discovered"
67	ok "repo discovered"
68	
69	step "start a task"
70	dev start demo --task auth --branch feat/auth --base main
71	WT="$HOME/Worktrees/demo/feat-auth"
72	[[ -d "$WT" ]]            || fail "worktree not created at $WT"
73	[[ -f "$WT/README.md" ]]  || fail "worktree has no tracked files"
74	[[ -f "$WT/.env" ]]       || fail "gitignored .env was not provisioned"
75	ok "worktree created at the templated path and provisioned"
76	
77	step "ls shows it hot"
78	dev ls | grep -q HOT || fail "task is not hot"
79	dev ls --json | grep -q '"branch": "feat/auth"' || fail "json output missing the branch"
80	ok "inventory reflects the task"
81	
82	step "commit work on the branch"
83	git -C "$WT" config user.email dev@example.test
84	git -C "$WT" config user.name  "dev e2e"
85	printf 'package auth\n' > "$WT/auth.go"
86	git -C "$WT" add auth.go
87	git -C "$WT" commit --quiet -m "feat: add auth"
88	ok "committed"
89	
90	step "park warm, with a next action"
91	dev park feat/auth --next "add the regression test"
92	dev ls | grep -q WARM                       || fail "task did not go warm"
93	dev ls | grep -q "add the regression test"  || fail "next action not recorded"
94	[[ -d "$WT" ]]                              || fail "a warm task must keep its worktree"
95	ok "parked warm, worktree intact"
96	
97	step "park cold with a push"
98	dev park feat/auth --cold --push
99	dev ls | grep -q COLD  || fail "task did not go cold"
100	[[ ! -d "$WT" ]]       || fail "a cold task must not keep its worktree"
101	git -C "$REPO" rev-parse --verify --quiet origin/feat/auth >/dev/null \
102	  || fail "the branch was not pushed"
103	ok "cold: worktree gone, work safe on the remote"
104	
105	step "resume rebuilds the worktree from the branch"
106	dev resume auth
107	[[ -f "$WT/auth.go" ]] || fail "resume did not restore the committed work"
108	dev ls | grep -q HOT   || fail "resumed task is not hot"
109	ok "rebuilt from origin"

## Shell integration

`/Users/david/Worktrees/dev-cli/feat-completion-and-brew/internal/cli/shell.go`

Relevant symbols:

- `posixInit`
- `fishInit`
- `newShellInitCmd`

Current commands:

```text
dev shell-init bash
dev shell-init zsh
dev shell-init fish
```

Behavior:

- Bash and Zsh receive the same POSIX `dev()` function.
- Fish receives a Fish function.
- The wrapper captures executable output.
- A successful `cd ...` directive is evaluated in the parent shell.
- Other multiline output is printed.
- `DEV_SHELL_INIT=1` is exported.
- `os.Executable()` is shell-quoted into the wrapper, so it calls a fixed underlying binary even though `dev` itself becomes a function.

Related symbols:

- `/Users/david/Worktrees/dev-cli/feat-completion-and-brew/internal/cli/app.go`

package cli

import (
	"fmt"
	"os"

	"github.com/spf13/cobra"
)

// zshInit and friends define the wrapper that makes `dev resume` able to leave
// the user *inside* the checkout.
//
// A process can never change its parent's working directory, so dev prints a
// `cd <path>` directive on stdout and the wrapper evaluates it. This is the
// same mechanism try-cli uses, and it is why `dev` is a shell function rather
// than only a binary.
const posixInit = `# dev shell integration — add to your rc file:
#   eval "$(dev shell-init %[2]s)"
export DEV_SHELL_INIT=1
dev() {
  local __dev_out __dev_status
  __dev_out="$(command %[1]s "$@")"
  __dev_status=$?
  if [ $__dev_status -eq 0 ] && [ "${__dev_out#cd }" != "$__dev_out" ]; then
    eval "$__dev_out"
  elif [ -n "$__dev_out" ]; then
    printf '%%s\n' "$__dev_out"
  fi
  return $__dev_status
}
`

const fishInit = `# dev shell integration — add to config.fish:
#   dev shell-init fish | source
set -gx DEV_SHELL_INIT 1
function dev
    set -l __dev_out (command %[1]s $argv)
    set -l __dev_status $status
    if test $__dev_status -eq 0; and string match -q 'cd *' -- "$__dev_out"
        eval $__dev_out
    else if test -n "$__dev_out"
        printf '%%s\n' $__dev_out
    end
    return $__dev_status
end
`

func newShellInitCmd(app *App) *cobra.Command {
	cmd := &cobra.Command{
		Use:   "shell-init <bash|zsh|fish>",
		Short: "Print the shell wrapper that lets dev change your directory",
		Long: `Print a shell function that wraps the dev binary.

dev commands that move you into a checkout (resume, try, wt open with the
"none" runtime) print a "cd <path>" directive rather than trying to change
directory themselves, because a child process cannot change its parent's
working directory. The wrapper evaluates that directive.

Add to your shell rc file:

    eval "$(dev shell-init zsh)"          # bash and zsh
    dev shell-init fish | source          # fish`,
		Args:      cobra.ExactArgs(1),
		ValidArgs: []string{"bash", "zsh", "fish"},
		RunE: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) error {
			self, err := os.Executable()
			if err != nil || self == "" {
				self = "dev"
			}
			switch args[0] {
			case "bash", "zsh":
				fmt.Fprintf(app.Out, posixInit, shellQuote(self), args[0])
			case "fish":
				fmt.Fprintf(app.Out, fishInit, shellQuote(self))
			default:
				return fmt.Errorf("unsupported shell %q: want bash, zsh or fish", args[0])
			}
			return nil
		},
	}
	// Completion is a sibling concern but belongs to the same "wire dev into
	// my shell" moment, so it hangs off this command.
	cmd.AddCommand(&cobra.Command{
		Use:       "completion <bash|zsh|fish>",
		Short:     "Print shell completions",
		Args:      cobra.ExactArgs(1),
		ValidArgs: []string{"bash", "zsh", "fish"},
		RunE: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) error {
			root := cmd.Root()
			switch args[0] {
			case "bash":
				return root.GenBashCompletionV2(app.Out, true)
			case "zsh":
				return root.GenZshCompletion(app.Out)
			case "fish":
				return root.GenFishCompletion(app.Out, true)
			}
			return fmt.Errorf("unsupported shell %q", args[0])
		},
	})
	return cmd
}

92	
93	## Adapting the default completion command
94	
95	Cobra provides a few options for the default `completion` command.  To configure such options you must set
96	the `CompletionOptions` field on the *root* command.
97	
98	To tell Cobra *not* to provide the default `completion` command:
99	```
100	rootCmd.CompletionOptions.DisableDefaultCmd = true
101	```
102	
103	To tell Cobra to mark the default `completion` command as *hidden*:
104	```
105	rootCmd.CompletionOptions.HiddenDefaultCmd = true
106	```
107	
108	To tell Cobra *not* to provide the user with the `--no-descriptions` flag to the completion sub-commands:
109	```
110	rootCmd.CompletionOptions.DisableNoDescFlag = true
111	```
112	
113	To tell Cobra to completely disable descriptions for completions:
114	```
115	rootCmd.CompletionOptions.DisableDescriptions = true
116	```
117	
118	# Customizing completions
119	
120	The generated completion scripts will automatically handle completing commands and flags.  However, you can make your completions much more powerful by providing information to complete your program's nouns and flag values.
121	
122	## Completion of nouns
123	
124	### Static completion of nouns
125	
126	Cobra allows you to provide a pre-defined list of completion choices for your nouns using the `ValidArgs` field.
127	For example, if you want `kubectl get [tab][tab]` to show a list of valid "nouns" you have to set them.
128	Some simplified code from `kubectl get` looks like:
129	
130	```go
131	validArgs = []string{ "pod", "node", "service", "replicationcontroller" }
132	
133	cmd := &cobra.Command{
134		Use:     "get [(-o|--output=)json|yaml|template|...] (RESOURCE [NAME] | RESOURCE/NAME ...)",
135		Short:   "Display one or many resources",
136		Long:    get_long,
137		Example: get_example,
138		Run: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {
```
</details></tool-use>

You can combine them with the bit-or operator such as `cobra.ShellCompDirectiveNoSpace | cobra.ShellCompDirectiveNoFileComp`

199	// have been provided (this implies none of the other directives).
200	ShellCompDirectiveDefault
201	
202	// Indicates an error occurred and completions should be ignored.
203	ShellCompDirectiveError
204	
205	// Indicates that the shell should not add a space after the completion,
206	// even if there is a single completion provided.
207	ShellCompDirectiveNoSpace
208	
209	// Indicates that the shell should not provide file completion even when
210	// no completion is provided.
211	ShellCompDirectiveNoFileComp
212	
213	// Indicates that the returned completions should be used as file extension filters.
214	// For example, to complete only files of the form *.json or *.yaml:
215	//    return []cobra.Completion{"yaml", "json"}, cobra.ShellCompDirectiveFilterFileExt
216	// For flags, using MarkFlagFilename() and MarkPersistentFlagFilename()
217	// is a shortcut to using this directive explicitly.
218	//
219	ShellCompDirectiveFilterFileExt
220	
221	// Indicates that only directory names should be provided in file completion.
222	// For example:
223	//    return nil, cobra.ShellCompDirectiveFilterDirs
224	// For flags, using MarkFlagDirname() is a shortcut to using this directive explicitly.
225	//
226	// To request directory names within another directory, the returned completions
227	// should specify a single directory name within which to search. For example,
228	// to complete directories within "themes/":
229	//    return []cobra.Completion{"themes"}, cobra.ShellCompDirectiveFilterDirs
230	//
231	ShellCompDirectiveFilterDirs
232	
233	// ShellCompDirectiveKeepOrder indicates that the shell should preserve the order

238	***Note***: When using the `ValidArgsFunction`, Cobra will call your registered function after having parsed all flags and arguments provided in the command-line.  You therefore don't need to do this parsing yourself.  For example, when a user calls `helm status --namespace my-rook-ns [tab][tab]`, Cobra will call your registered `ValidArgsFunction` after having parsed the `--namespace` flag, as it would have done when calling the `RunE` function.
239	
240	#### Debugging
241	
242	Cobra achieves dynamic completion through the use of a hidden command called by the completion script.  To debug your Go completion code, you can call this hidden command directly:
243	```bash
244	$ helm __complete status har<ENTER>
245	harbor
246	:4
247	Completion ended with directive: ShellCompDirectiveNoFileComp # This is on stderr
248	```
249	***Important:*** If the noun to complete is empty (when the user has not yet typed any letters of that noun), you must pass an empty parameter to the `__complete` command:
250	```bash
251	$ helm __complete status ""<ENTER>
252	harbor
253	notary
254	rook
255	thanos
256	:4
257	Completion ended with directive: ShellCompDirectiveNoFileComp # This is on stderr
258	```
259	Calling the `__complete` command directly allows you to run the Go debugger to troubleshoot your code.  You can also add printouts to your code; Cobra provides the following functions to use for printouts in Go completion code:
260	```go
261	// Prints to the completion script debug file (if BASH_COMP_DEBUG_FILE
262	// is set to a file path) and optionally prints to stderr.
263	cobra.CompDebug(msg string, printToStdErr bool)
264	cobra.CompDebugln(msg string, printToStdErr bool)
265	
266	// Prints to the completion script debug file (if BASH_COMP_DEBUG_FILE
267	// is set to a file path) and to stderr.
268	cobra.CompError(msg string)
269	cobra.CompErrorln(msg string)
270	```
271	***Important:*** You should **not** leave traces that print directly to stdout in your completion code as they will be interpreted as completion choices by the completion script.  Instead, use the cobra-provided debugging traces functions mentioned above.
272	
273	## Completions for flags
274	
275	### Mark flags as required
276	
277	Most of the time completions will only show sub-commands. But if a flag is required to make a sub-command work, you probably want it to show up when the user types [tab][tab].  You can mark a flag as 'Required' like so:
278	
279	```go
280	cmd.MarkFlagRequired("pod")
281	cmd.MarkFlagRequired("container")
282	```
283	
284	and you'll get something like
285	
286	```bash
287	$ kubectl exec [tab][tab]
288	-c            --container=  -p            --pod=
289	```
290	
291	### Specify dynamic flag completion
292	
293	As for nouns, Cobra provides a way of defining dynamic completion of flags.  To provide a Go function that Cobra will execute when it needs the list of completion choices for a flag, you must register the function using the `command.RegisterFlagCompletionFunc()` function.
294	
295	```go
296	flagName := "output"
297	cmd.RegisterFlagCompletionFunc(flagName, func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string, toComplete string) ([]cobra.Completion, cobra.ShellCompDirective) {
298		return []cobra.Completion{"json", "table", "yaml"}, cobra.ShellCompDirectiveDefault
299	})
300	```
301	Notice that calling `RegisterFlagCompletionFunc()` is done through the `command` with which the flag is associated.  In our example this dynamic completion will give results like so:
302	
303	```bash
304	$ helm status --output [tab][tab]
305	json table yaml
306	```
307	
308	#### Change the default ShellCompDirective
309	
310	When no completion function is registered for a leaf command or for a flag, Cobra will
311	automatically use `ShellCompDirectiveDefault`, which will invoke the shell's filename completion.
312	This implies that when file completion does not apply to a leaf command or to a flag (the command
313	or flag does not operate on a filename), turning off file completion requires you to register a
314	completion function for that command/flag.
315	For example:
316	
317	```go
318	cmd.RegisterFlagCompletionFunc("flag-name", cobra.NoFileCompletions)
319	```
320	
321	If you find that there are more situations where file completion should be turned off than
322	when it is applicable, you can recursively change the default `ShellCompDirective` for a command
323	and its subcommands to `ShellCompDirectiveNoFileComp`:
324	
325	```go
326	cmd.CompletionOptions.SetDefaultShellCompDirective(ShellCompDirectiveNoFileComp)
327	```
328	
329	If doing so, keep in mind that you should instead register a completion function for leaf commands or
330	flags where file completion is applicable. For example:
331	
332	```go
333	cmd.RegisterFlagCompletionFunc("flag-name", cobra.FixedCompletions(nil, ShellCompDirectiveDefault))
334	```
335	
336	To change the default directive for the entire program, set the DefaultShellCompDirective on the root command.
337

Author: Da-Wei Lee <daviddwlee84@gmail.com>
Date:   Thu Aug 27 12:00:36 2026 +0800

    feat: dev CLI for managing work in progress across repos
    
    dev is a thin glue layer over git, worktrees, forges and agent runtimes.
    It keeps four things separate that otherwise collapse into one: the remote
    (durable code state), worktrees (disposable checkouts), herdr/tmux (per-host
    runtime) and dev itself (human intent).
    
    Everything derivable from git or the runtime is derived live; dev persists
    only what git cannot answer — a task's state, owner and next action — as one
    TOML file per task, so a state directory can be a git repo and merge cleanly
    across machines.
    
    The problem it solves: when a multiplexer's sidebar is the only record of
    what you are working on, nothing can be closed without losing the thread,
    so it grows until it stops being scannable.
    
    - HOT/WARM/COLD/DONE task lifecycle with start/park/resume/done/sweep. Going
      cold is safe because the branch is the identity and the directory a cache.
    - One worktree ownership rule: dev owns anything a human may return to,
      Claude Code keeps .claude/worktrees for turn-scoped isolation. dev creates
      checkouts with git and asks herdr only to open them, so the configurable
      path policy holds on machines without herdr.
    - Worktree provisioning: gitignored-file copying, opt-in symlinks and
      lockfile-detected setup commands, overridable per repo via .dev.toml.
    - Pluggable runtime adapters (herdr, tmux, none) sharing one contract suite.
    - Repo discovery and gh/glab-backed clone, create, sync — both CLIs optional.
    - Dated experiments via try, promoted into real projects via graduate.
    - Activity heatmap from a session sampler, git backfill and WakaTime import.
    - Bundled agent skill embedded in the binary, with a command reference
      generated from the live command tree so the two cannot drift.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
    Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01KfgWSELDAofucwXjMMxBao

commit f3af72e6ae67b84c1085fbbfb50889c15827a6a0
Author: Da-Wei Lee <daviddwlee84@gmail.com>
Date:   Thu Aug 27 12:00:36 2026 +0800

    feat: dev CLI for managing work in progress across repos
    
    dev is a thin glue layer over git, worktrees, forges and agent runtimes.
    It keeps four things separate that otherwise collapse into one: the remote
    (durable code state), worktrees (disposable checkouts), herdr/tmux (per-host
    runtime) and dev itself (human intent).
    
    Everything derivable from git or the runtime is derived live; dev persists
    only what git cannot answer — a task's state, owner and next action — as one
    TOML file per task, so a state directory can be a git repo and merge cleanly
    across machines.
    
    The problem it solves: when a multiplexer's sidebar is the only record of
    what you are working on, nothing can be closed without losing the thread,
    so it grows until it stops being scannable.
    
    - HOT/WARM/COLD/DONE task lifecycle with start/park/resume/done/sweep. Going
      cold is safe because the branch is the identity and the directory a cache.
    - One worktree ownership rule: dev owns anything a human may return to,
      Claude Code keeps .claude/worktrees for turn-scoped isolation. dev creates
      checkouts with git and asks herdr only to open them, so the configurable
      path policy holds on machines without herdr.
    - Worktree provisioning: gitignored-file copying, opt-in symlinks and
      lockfile-detected setup commands, overridable per repo via .dev.toml.
    - Pluggable runtime adapters (herdr, tmux, none) sharing one contract suite.
    - Repo discovery and gh/glab-backed clone, create, sync — both CLIs optional.
    - Dated experiments via try, promoted into real projects via graduate.
    - Activity heatmap from a session sampler, git backfill and WakaTime import.
    - Bundled agent skill embedded in the binary, with a command reference
      generated from the live command tree so the two cannot drift.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
    Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01KfgWSELDAofucwXjMMxBao

3	package bootstrap

5	import (
6		"os"
7		"syscall"
8	)
9	
10	// sameFilesystem reports whether two existing paths live on the same device,
11	// which is the prerequisite for an atomic rename.
12	func sameFilesystem(a, b string) bool {
13		ai, err := os.Stat(a)
14		if err != nil {
15			return false
16		}
17		bi, err := os.Stat(b)
18		if err != nil {
19			return false
20		}
21		as, aok := ai.Sys().(*syscall.Stat_t)
22		bs, bok := bi.Sys().(*syscall.Stat_t)
23		return aok && bok && as.Dev == bs.Dev
24	}
25

The API-level picture is now clear: Cobra initializes a top-level `completion` command during `ExecuteC()` unless disabled, and this root does not disable it. Consequently the CLI has two generators—Cobra’s automatic `dev completion {bash,zsh,fish,powershell}` and the manually nested `dev shell-init completion {bash,zsh,fish}`—but only the shell-wrapper path is documented in project files, and only wrapper output is tested.

34	func MakeID(repo, branch string) string {
35		clean := func(s string) string {
36			s = idUnsafe.ReplaceAllString(s, "-")
37			for strings.Contains(s, "--") {
38				s = strings.ReplaceAll(s, "--", "-")
39			}
40			return strings.Trim(s, "-._")
41		}
42		r, b := clean(repo), clean(branch)
43		if r == "" {
44			r = "repo"
45		}
46		if b == "" {
47			b = "branch"
48		}
49		return r + "__" + b
50	}

54	// Save writes a task, stamping Updated (and Created on first write).
55	func (s *Store) Save(t *Task) error {
56		if t.ID == "" {
57			t.ID = MakeID(t.Repo, t.Branch)
58		}
59		if err := t.Validate(); err != nil {
60			return err
61		}
62		now := time.Now().UTC().Truncate(time.Second)
63		if t.Created.IsZero() {
64			t.Created = now
65		}
66		t.Updated = now
67	
68		if err := os.MkdirAll(s.Dir, 0o755); err != nil {
69			return fmt.Errorf("create state dir: %w", err)
70		}
71		// Write to a temp file and rename, so an interrupted write can never leave
72		// a half-parsed task behind.
73		tmp, err := os.CreateTemp(s.Dir, "."+t.ID+".*.tmp")
74		if err != nil {
75			return err
76		}
77		defer os.Remove(tmp.Name())
78		enc := toml.NewEncoder(tmp)
79		if err := enc.Encode(t); err != nil {
80			tmp.Close()
81			return fmt.Errorf("encode task %s: %w", t.ID, err)
82		}
83		if err := tmp.Close(); err != nil {
84			return err
85		}
86		if err := os.Chmod(tmp.Name(), 0o644); err != nil {
87			return err
88		}
89		return os.Rename(tmp.Name(), s.path(t.ID))
90	}

1	// Package repo discovers the repositories a user actually owns by walking the
2	// configured scan roots. It answers "what projects do I have?", which is a
3	// different question from "what am I working on?" — that one belongs to
4	// package task.
5	package repo
6	
7	import (
8		"context"
9		"io/fs"
10		"os"
11		"path/filepath"
12		"sort"
13		"strings"
14	
15		"github.com/daviddwlee84/dev-cli/internal/gitx"
16	)
17	
18	// Repo is one discovered repository.
19	type Repo struct {
20		// Name is the directory basename, which is how users refer to it.
21		Name string
22		// Path is the absolute path reached through the scan root. It may be a
23		// symlink from a bootstrap index; commands intentionally keep that human
24		// navigation path rather than replacing it with the physical one.
25		Path string
26		// RealPath is the physical checkout path.
27		RealPath string
28		// Symlink reports that Path is an alias to RealPath.
29		Symlink bool
30		// Root is the scan root it was found under.
31		Root string
32		// Category is the path between the scan root and the repo ("Quant",
33		// "Web/Frontend"), empty for a repo sitting directly in the root. It is
34		// human organisation metadata, preserved for `dev graduate` to place new
35		// projects consistently.
36		Category string
37		// CommonDir is Git's shared administrative directory. Its worktrees/
38		// children let inventory count linked checkouts without another git
39		// process per repository.
40		CommonDir string
41		// Bare reports a bare repository (a worktree hub).
42		Bare bool
43		// HasGit distinguishes a real repo from a plain directory that was found
44		// in a scan root; non-repos are reported so `dev repo list` can offer to
45		// initialise them.
46		HasGit bool
47	}
48	
49	// Display renders "Category/Name" or just "Name".
50	func (r Repo) Display() string {
51		if r.Category == "" {
52			return r.Name
53		}
54		return r.Category + "/" + r.Name
55	}
56	
57	// Options tunes discovery.
58	type Options struct {
59		// MaxDepth limits how deep below a scan root a repo may be found. The
60		// default layout is <root>/<Category>/<Repo>, so 2 suffices; 3 leaves room
61		// for a nested grouping without walking an entire home directory.
62		MaxDepth int
63		// IncludeNonRepos reports plain directories alongside repositories.
64		IncludeNonRepos bool
65	}
66	
67	// DefaultOptions is the discovery configuration used by dev's commands.
68	func DefaultOptions() Options { return Options{MaxDepth: 3} }
69	
70	// skipDirs are never descended into. These are large, never contain a project
71	// the user organises by hand, and walking them dominates scan time.
72	var skipDirs = map[string]bool{
73		"node_modules": true, ".venv": true, "venv": true, "target": true,
74		"vendor": true, "__pycache__": true, ".tox": true, "dist": true,
75		"build": true, ".next": true, ".cache": true, ".terraform": true,
76		"Library": true, ".Trash": true,
77	}
78	
79	// Discover walks every root and returns the repositories found, sorted by
80	// display name. Unreadable directories are skipped rather than fatal — a scan
81	// root that has been unmounted must not break `dev ls`.
82	func Discover(ctx context.Context, roots []string, opts Options) ([]Repo, error) {
83		if opts.MaxDepth <= 0 {
84			opts.MaxDepth = DefaultOptions().MaxDepth
85		}
86		seen := map[string]bool{}
87		// clone identities stop a physical path and a symlink index from showing
88		// the same repository twice. The first scan root wins, which lets users
89		// choose whether the curated index or the physical hierarchy is their UI
90		// simply by ordering scan_roots.
91		identities := map[string]bool{}
92		var out []Repo
93	
94		for _, root := range roots {
95			info, err := os.Stat(root)
96			if err != nil || !info.IsDir() {
97				continue // a missing scan root is normal on a fresh machine
98			}
99			rootClean := filepath.Clean(root)
100	
101			err = filepath.WalkDir(rootClean, func(path string, d fs.DirEntry, err error) error {
102				if err != nil {
103					return nil // unreadable entry: skip, keep walking
104				}
105				if ctx.Err() != nil {
106					return ctx.Err()
107				}
108				if path == rootClean {
109					return nil
110				}
111				name := d.Name()
112				isLink := d.Type()&os.ModeSymlink != 0
113				isDir := d.IsDir()
114				if isLink {
115					// WalkDir does not follow symlinks. Inspect a direct symlink to
116					// a repository, but do not recurse through arbitrary symlinked
117					// containers — bootstrap does that with cycle detection.
118					if info, err := os.Stat(path); err == nil {
119						isDir = info.IsDir()
120					}
121				}
122				if !isDir {
123					return nil
124				}
125				if skipDirs[name] || (strings.HasPrefix(name, ".") && name != ".bare") {
126					return filepath.SkipDir
127				}
128	
129				rel, _ := filepath.Rel(rootClean, path)
130				depth := len(strings.Split(rel, string(filepath.Separator)))
131	
132				if isRepoDir(path) {
133					real, _ := filepath.EvalSymlinks(path)
134					if real == "" {
135						real = path
136					}
137					bare := isBareDir(path)
138					identity, commonDir := real, real
139					if !bare {
140						if g, err := gitx.Discover(ctx, path); err == nil {
141							// A linked worktree is execution state, not another
142							// project in the repo inventory.
143							if g.IsLinkedWorktree {
144								return filepath.SkipDir
145							}
146							identity, commonDir = g.GitCommonDir, g.GitCommonDir
147							real = g.MainRoot
148						}
149					}
150					if !seen[path] && !identities[identity] {
151						seen[path], identities[identity] = true, true
152						out = append(out, Repo{
153							Name:      name,
154							Path:      path,
155							RealPath:  real,
156							Symlink:   isLink,
157							Root:      rootClean,
158							Category:  filepath.ToSlash(filepath.Dir(rel)),
159							CommonDir: commonDir,
160							Bare:      bare,
161							HasGit:    true,
162						})
163					}
164					// Never descend into a repo: its subdirectories are source
165					// code, and any nested .git is a submodule or a worktree that
166					// belongs to this repo, not a project of its own.
167					return filepath.SkipDir
168				}
169				if depth >= opts.MaxDepth {
170					return filepath.SkipDir
171				}
172				if opts.IncludeNonRepos && depth == 1 {
173					if !seen[path] {
174						seen[path] = true
175						out = append(out, Repo{Name: name, Path: path, Root: rootClean, Category: ""})
176					}
177				}
178				return nil
179			})
180			if err != nil && ctx.Err() != nil {
181				return out, ctx.Err()
182			}
183		}
184	
185		for i := range out {

189		}
190		sort.Slice(out, func(i, j int) bool {
191			if out[i].Name != out[j].Name {

193			}

230	// initCompleteCmd adds a special hidden command that can be used to request custom completions.
231	func (c *Command) initCompleteCmd(args []string) {
232		completeCmd := &Command{
233			Use:                   fmt.Sprintf("%s [command-line]", ShellCompRequestCmd),
234			Aliases:               []string{ShellCompNoDescRequestCmd},
235			DisableFlagsInUseLine: true,
236			Hidden:                true,
237			DisableFlagParsing:    true,
238			Args:                  MinimumNArgs(1),
239			Short:                 "Request shell completion choices for the specified command-line",
240			Long: fmt.Sprintf("%[2]s is a special command that is used by the shell completion logic\n%[1]s",
241				"to request completion choices for the specified command-line.", ShellCompRequestCmd),
242			Run: func(cmd *Command, args []string) {
243				finalCmd, completions, directive, err := cmd.getCompletions(args)
244				if err != nil {
245					CompErrorln(err.Error())
246					// Keep going for multiple reasons:
247					// 1- There could be some valid completions even though there was an error
248					// 2- Even without completions, we need to print the directive
249				}
250	
251				noDescriptions := cmd.CalledAs() == ShellCompNoDescRequestCmd
252				if !noDescriptions {
253					if doDescriptions, err := strconv.ParseBool(getEnvConfig(cmd, configEnvVarSuffixDescriptions)); err == nil {
254						noDescriptions = !doDescriptions
255					}
256				}
257				noActiveHelp := GetActiveHelpConfig(finalCmd) == activeHelpGlobalDisable
258				out := finalCmd.OutOrStdout()
259				for _, comp := range completions {
260					if noActiveHelp && strings.HasPrefix(comp, activeHelpMarker) {
261						// Remove all activeHelp entries if it's disabled.
262						continue
263					}
264					if noDescriptions {
265						// Remove any description that may be included following a tab character.
266						comp = strings.SplitN(comp, "\t", 2)[0]
267					}
268	
269					// Make sure we only write the first line to the output.
270					// This is needed if a description contains a linebreak.
271					// Otherwise the shell scripts will interpret the other lines as new flags
272					// and could therefore provide a wrong completion.
273					comp = strings.SplitN(comp, "\n", 2)[0]
274	
275					// Finally trim the completion.  This is especially important to get rid
276					// of a trailing tab when there are no description following it.
277					// For example, a sub-command without a description should not be completed
278					// with a tab at the end (or else zsh will show a -- following it
279					// although there is no description).
280					comp = strings.TrimSpace(comp)
281	
282					// Print each possible completion to the output for the completion script to consume.
283					fmt.Fprintln(out, comp)
284				}
285	
286				// As the last printout, print the completion directive for the completion script to parse.
287				// The directive integer must be that last character following a single colon (:).
288				// The completion script expects :<directive>
289				fmt.Fprintf(out, ":%d\n", directive)
290	
291				// Print some helpful info to stderr for the user to understand.
292				// Output from stderr must be ignored by the completion script.
293				fmt.Fprintf(finalCmd.ErrOrStderr(), "Completion ended with directive: %s\n", directive.string())
294			},
295		}
296		c.AddCommand(completeCmd)
297		subCmd, _, err := c.Find(args)
298		if err != nil || subCmd.Name() != ShellCompRequestCmd {
299			// Only create this special command if it is actually being called.
300			// This reduces possible side-effects of creating such a command;
301			// for example, having this command would cause problems to a
302			// cobra program that only consists of the root command, since this
303			// command would cause the root command to suddenly have a subcommand.
304			c.RemoveCommand(completeCmd)
305		}
306	}

1	package cli
2	
3	import (
4		"fmt"
5		"io"
6		"strings"
7		"time"
8		"unicode/utf8"
9	)
10	
11	// Table renders aligned columns. It measures width in runes rather than bytes
12	// so the CJK repo and branch names in a real inventory line up.
13	type Table struct {
14		head []string
15		rows [][]string
16	}
17	
18	// NewTable starts a table with the given header.
19	func NewTable(header ...string) *Table { return &Table{head: header} }
20	
21	// Add appends a row. Short rows are padded, long ones are truncated to the
22	// header width so a stray field can never shift the whole table.
23	func (t *Table) Add(cells ...string) {
24		row := make([]string, len(t.head))
25		copy(row, cells)
26		t.rows = append(t.rows, row)
27	}
28	
29	// Len reports the number of data rows.
30	func (t *Table) Len() int { return len(t.rows) }
31	
32	// Render writes the table, sizing every column to its widest cell.
33	func (t *Table) Render(w io.Writer) {
34		if len(t.rows) == 0 {
35			return
36		}
37		widths := make([]int, len(t.head))
38		for i, h := range t.head {
39			widths[i] = width(h)
40		}
41		for _, r := range t.rows {
42			for i, c := range r {
43				if n := width(c); n > widths[i] {
44					widths[i] = n
45				}
46			}
47		}
48		writeRow(w, t.head, widths)
49		for _, r := range t.rows {
50			writeRow(w, r, widths)
51		}
52	}
53	
54	func writeRow(w io.Writer, cells []string, widths []int) {
55		var b strings.Builder
56		for i, c := range cells {
57			if i == len(cells)-1 {
58				b.WriteString(c) // never pad the last column
59				break
60			}
61			b.WriteString(c)
62			b.WriteString(strings.Repeat(" ", widths[i]-width(c)+2))
63		}
64		fmt.Fprintln(w, strings.TrimRight(b.String(), " "))
65	}
66	
67	// width counts display columns, treating wide CJK runes as two.
68	func width(s string) int {
69		n := 0
70		for _, r := range s {
71			if isWide(r) {
72				n += 2
73			} else {
74				n++
75			}
76		}
77		return n
78	}
79	
80	func isWide(r rune) bool {
81		switch {
82		case r >= 0x1100 && r <= 0x115F, // Hangul Jamo
83			r >= 0x2E80 && r <= 0xA4CF, // CJK radicals through Yi
84			r >= 0xAC00 && r <= 0xD7A3, // Hangul syllables
85			r >= 0xF900 && r <= 0xFAFF, // CJK compatibility ideographs
```

8	// Worktree is one entry of `git worktree list --porcelain`.
9	type Worktree struct {
10		Path string
11		// Head is the commit the worktree is checked out at.
12		Head string
13		// Branch is the short branch name, empty when detached.
14		Branch   string
15		Detached bool
16		Bare     bool
17		// Locked reports a `git worktree lock`; Prunable reports a checkout whose
18		// directory has gone missing. Both block a plain remove.
19		Locked         bool
20		LockedReason   string
21		Prunable       bool
22		PrunableReason string
23		// Main reports the primary (non-linked) checkout.
24		Main bool
25	}
26	
27	// Worktrees lists every worktree of the repository containing dir, in git's
28	// own order: the main checkout first, then linked worktrees.
29	func Worktrees(ctx context.Context, dir string) ([]Worktree, error) {
30		out, err := run(ctx, dir, "worktree", "list", "--porcelain")
31		if err != nil {
32			return nil, err
33		}
34		var (
35			list []Worktree
36			cur  *Worktree
37		)
38		flush := func() {
39			if cur != nil {
40				list = append(list, *cur)
41				cur = nil
42			}
43		}
44		for _, line := range strings.Split(out, "\n") {
45			if line == "" { // records are blank-line separated
46				flush()
47				continue
48			}
49			key, val, _ := strings.Cut(line, " ")
50			switch key {
51			case "worktree":
52				flush()
53				cur = &Worktree{Path: val, Main: len(list) == 0}
54			case "HEAD":
55				if cur != nil {
56					cur.Head = val
57				}
58			case "branch":
59				if cur != nil {
60					cur.Branch = strings.TrimPrefix(val, "refs/heads/")
61				}
62			case "detached":
63				if cur != nil {
64					cur.Detached = true
65				}
66			case "bare":
67				if cur != nil {
68					cur.Bare = true
69				}
70			case "locked":
71				if cur != nil {
72					cur.Locked, cur.LockedReason = true, val
73				}
74			case "prunable":
75				if cur != nil {
76					cur.Prunable, cur.PrunableReason = true, val
77				}
78			}
79		}
80		flush()

532	// commandRunnable resolves the command's first word on PATH, expanding a

534	func commandRunnable(run string, interactive bool) func() bool {
535		// Availability is stable for the lifetime of one dashboard. In particular,
536		// probing an interactive alias starts a login shell; doing that on every
537		// render would turn a 60fps UI into a shell-launch benchmark.
538		var once sync.Once
539		available := false
540		return func() bool {
541			once.Do(func() { available = checkCommandRunnable(run, interactive) })
542			return available
543		}
544	}

546	func checkCommandRunnable(run string, interactive bool) bool {
547		word := firstWord(run)
548		if strings.HasPrefix(word, "$") {
549			word = os.Getenv(strings.TrimPrefix(word, "$"))
550			if word == "" {
551				return false
552			}
553			word = firstWord(word)
554		}
555		if word == "" {
556			return false
557		}
558		if interactive {
559			// Ask the configured shell after it loads its rc files; LookPath
560			// cannot see aliases or functions.
561			ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 3*time.Second)
562			defer cancel()
563			probe := exec.CommandContext(ctx, shellPath(), "-lic",
564				`command -v "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1`, "dev-tool-probe", word)

567		if filepath.IsAbs(word) {
568			_, err := os.Stat(word)
569			return err == nil
570		}
571		_, err := exec.LookPath(word)
572		return err == nil
573	}

12	type PostCreate struct {

17	// UnmarshalTOML implements toml.Unmarshaler.
18	func (p *PostCreate) UnmarshalTOML(v any) error {
19		switch t := v.(type) {
20		case string:
21			if t != "auto" {
22				return fmt.Errorf("post_create: %q is not a valid string form (use \"auto\" or a list of commands)", t)
23			}
24			*p = PostCreate{Auto: true}
25			return nil
26		case []any:
27			cmds := make([]string, 0, len(t))
28			for i, e := range t {
29				s, ok := e.(string)
30				if !ok {
31					return fmt.Errorf("post_create[%d]: want a command string, got %T", i, e)
32				}
33				cmds = append(cmds, s)
34			}
35			*p = PostCreate{Commands: cmds}
36			return nil
37		default:
38			return fmt.Errorf("post_create: want \"auto\" or a list of command strings, got %T", v)
39		}
40	}
41	
42	// MarshalTOML implements toml.Marshaler so a config round-trips.
43	func (p PostCreate) MarshalTOML() ([]byte, error) {
44		if p.Auto {
45			return []byte(`"auto"`), nil
46		}
47		out := []byte("[")
48		for i, c := range p.Commands {
49			if i > 0 {
50				out = append(out, ", "...)
51			}
52			out = append(out, fmt.Sprintf("%q", c)...)
53		}
54		return append(out, ']'), nil
55	}

57	// Duration is a time.Duration written in TOML as a Go duration string
58	// ("10m", "90s"), which is friendlier than a bare number of seconds.
59	type Duration struct{ time.Duration }
60	
61	// UnmarshalTOML implements toml.Unmarshaler.
62	func (d *Duration) UnmarshalTOML(v any) error {
63		switch t := v.(type) {
64		case string:
65			parsed, err := time.ParseDuration(t)
66			if err != nil {
67				return fmt.Errorf("duration %q: %w", t, err)
68			}
69			d.Duration = parsed
70			return nil
71		case int64:
72			d.Duration = time.Duration(t) * time.Second
73			return nil
74		default:
75			return fmt.Errorf("duration: want a string like \"10m\", got %T", v)
76		}
77	}

79	// MarshalTOML implements toml.Marshaler.

The remaining integration nuance is favorable: Cobra’s generated scripts invoke the command token (`dev`) rather than hard-coding a binary path, so they can operate through the `dev()` wrapper function emitted by `shell-init`. The wrapper itself pins `command <absolute os.Executable()>`, preserves multiline stdout, and exports `DEV_SHELL_INIT`; however, `doctor` detects only that wrapper marker, not whether completion has been loaded.

_**Agent - sidechain (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-08-27 14:22:32Z)**_

The installation split is now clear: `go_tools` is globally included but no-ops unless mise provides Go, and it is explicitly Linux-only; macOS must use the shared Brewfile to avoid `~/.local/bin` shadowing the brew binary. For `dev-cli`, this distinction matters because the repository is `github.com/daviddwlee84/dev-cli`, the executable is `dev`, and the generated completion cache must therefore be keyed as `dev`, not `dev-cli`.

55	set -e
56	export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
57	
58	# Override locale to a safe default so ansible can start even before locale
59	# packages are installed. Prefer C.UTF-8 (universal since glibc 2.35) but
60	# fall back to en_US.UTF-8 on CentOS 7 (glibc 2.17) where C.UTF-8 is
61	# missing and `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8` triggers
62	# `Ansible could not initialize the preferred locale: unsupported locale
63	# setting`. Fall through silently if neither is available — the parent
64	# shell's LANG/LC_ALL (e.g. set via ENV in Dockerfile.centos7) wins.
65	if locale -a 2>/dev/null | grep -qiE '^C\.utf-?8$'; then
66	    export LC_ALL=C.UTF-8
67	    export LANG=C.UTF-8
68	elif locale -a 2>/dev/null | grep -qiE '^en_US\.utf-?8$'; then
69	    export LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8
70	    export LANG=en_US.UTF-8
71	fi

73	# --- Shared sudo session (see scripts/lib/sudo_shared.sh for full docs)
74	# Inlined at template-render time so this script carries the helper body.
75	# bootstrap has already prompted + spawned a watchdog in the normal flow;
76	# the idempotent `sudo_session_init` below just re-exports the env vars
77	# and (re)registers the INT/TERM/HUP abort trap. It will prompt here only
78	# when the user ran ansible manually without the bootstrap phase.
79	{{ include "scripts/lib/sudo_shared.sh" }}
80	# --- end sudo helper
81	
82	# Whether ANY sudo surface is exercised in this run. Linux ansible always
83	# needs sudo unless noRoot. On macOS only the input_method role needs sudo.
84	NEED_SUDO={{ if or (and (eq .chezmoi.os "linux") (not .noRoot)) (and (eq .chezmoi.os "darwin") .installInputMethod) }}1{{ else }}0{{ end }}
85	
86	# Setup Homebrew PATH so brew subprocesses can find sibling tools like git-lfs.
87	{{ if eq .chezmoi.os "darwin" -}}
88	if [[ -f /opt/homebrew/bin/brew ]]; then
89	    eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"
90	elif [[ -f /usr/local/bin/brew ]]; then
91	    eval "$(/usr/local/bin/brew shellenv)"
92	fi
93	{{ else -}}
94	# Linuxbrew — guard on the binary, not the dir. A failed Homebrew install
95	# leaves the /home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew/ tree behind (sudo'd by the
96	# installer) without the brew binary, and `eval "$(.../bin/brew shellenv)"`
97	# would then noisy-fail on every chezmoi apply. See
98	# pitfalls/bootstrap-no-tty-sudo-prompt-skipped.md → CentOS 7 brew note.
99	if [[ -x /home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew/bin/brew ]]; then
100	    eval "$(/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew/bin/brew shellenv)"
101	elif [[ -x "$HOME/.linuxbrew/bin/brew" ]]; then
102	    eval "$("$HOME/.linuxbrew/bin/brew" shellenv)"
103	fi
104	{{ end -}}

106	# Install-only apply doesn't need Homebrew's periodic auto-update, whose `brew
107	# update` (git fetch) can hang for many minutes on a constrained network/mirror
108	# — it stalled the opt-in calibre cask install for ~34 min. Inherited by the
109	# ansible community.general.homebrew{,_cask} subprocesses. Matches
110	# run_onchange_after_30_brew_bundle.sh.tmpl.
111	export HOMEBREW_NO_AUTO_UPDATE=1
112	
113	{{ if .useChineseMirror -}}
114	# GFW mirrors (useChineseMirror=true) — exported so ansible subprocesses
115	# (community.general.homebrew, mise, rustup, gem) inherit them. Without
116	# this, ghcr.io bottle downloads frequently fail with
117	# `curl: (18) Transferred a partial file` and rust-lang.org / nodejs.org
118	# downloads time out on constrained networks.
119	# Ref: https://mirrors.bfsu.edu.cn/help/homebrew-bottles/

49	## Install order
50	
51	Five phases in chronological order. Anything earlier MUST be present
52	before the next phase can run.
53	
54	```
55	┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
56	│ Phase 0 — Bootstrap (run_once_before_*)                                 │
57	│   curl-installer: Homebrew, uv, mise                                    │
58	│   apt: build-essential, git, curl (Linux prereqs for Linuxbrew)         │
59	│   apt: libffi-dev, libyaml-dev, python3-dev (Linux non-noRoot only)     │
60	│   uv: ansible-core (pinned Python 3.13)                                 │
61	│   ansible-galaxy: community.general collection                          │
62	│   mise: install runtimes from ~/.config/mise/config.toml                │
63	└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
64	                                  │
65	                                  ▼
66	┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
67	│ Phase 1 — chezmoi apply (config file deploy)                            │
68	│   Deploys dot_* files; doesn't install tools directly                   │
69	└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
70	                                  │
71	                                  ▼
72	┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
73	│ Phase 2 — Ansible (run_onchange_after_20_ansible_roles)                 │
74	│   Runs all 26 roles; each dispatches to its underlying manager          │
75	│   (brew / apt / mise / uv / npm / cargo / gem / dotnet / curl / gh-rel) │
76	└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
77	                                  │
78	                                  ▼
79	┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
80	│ Phase 3 — Brew bundle (run_onchange_after_30_brew_bundle)               │
81	│   `brew bundle --no-upgrade` against ~/.config/homebrew/Brewfile*       │
82	│   Mostly GUI casks (macOS); skipped unless Brew/AI/gaming apps enabled  │
83	└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
84	                                  │
85	                                  ▼
86	┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
87	│ Phase 4 — Per-application onchange scripts                              │
88	│   Completion regen (run_after_50_generate_completions)                  │
89	│   bat theme cache (run_onchange_after_25_bat_theme)                     │
90	│   ble.sh compile (run_onchange_after_26_install_blesh)                  │
91	│   Global skills restore (run_onchange_after_40_install_global_skills)   │
92	└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
93	```
94	
95	The bootstrap is **single-source-of-truth** for the foundational tools
96	that everything else depends on. If you find yourself wanting to add
97	`mise` / `uv` / Homebrew elsewhere, the answer is almost always "extend
98	the bootstrap, then assume it in the role". The Linux noRoot path
99	(`profile=ubuntu_server` or RHEL/CentOS without sudo) skips the apt
100	prereqs and Linuxbrew, falling back to per-tool curl-installers and
101	GitHub releases — coverage is intentionally narrower (no GUI, no
102	system-wide installs).
103	
104	---
```

175	A fake `brew` stub (`#!/bin/sh` + `exit 0`) — historically recommended in

232	Linuxbrew (when present), or GitHub releases. See each role for the

241	Homebrew 6+ refuses formulae/casks from untrusted third-party taps. Role-driven
242	taps must run a `brew tap-info <tap>` → `brew trust <tap>` check before installing
243	from that tap; Brewfile taps are handled by the brew-bundle run-script before it
244	calls `brew bundle`. See

247	**Adding via homebrew**: prefer a brew formula/cask only when the tool
248	is macOS-shipped and Linux equivalents go via apt or release tarball.
249	Linux-first tools rarely belong in the Brewfile.

253	`scripts/upgrade_tools.sh::_uv_install_style` (and mirrored helpers in

 `/Users/david/.local/share/chezmoi/docs/this_repo/upgrades.md`

```text
1	# Upgrades — Explicit, Opt-in Tool Refresh
2	
3	> How to actually move installed tools forward on a machine managed by this repo, and why `chezmoi apply` deliberately will *not* do that for you.
4	
5	> **See also**: [`tool-managers.md`](tool-managers.md) — the install-side companion to this doc. It maps every tool in the repo to its install mechanism (which manager owns it, where it lands, per-OS dispatch). When you're trying to figure out "why doesn't `just upgrade-X` move tool Y forward?", that's where the coverage gaps are documented.
6	
7	## Why install and upgrade are split
8	
9	`chezmoi apply` (and the ansible phase it triggers) is **install-only by design**. Ansible roles use `state: present` + `creates:` so that running `chezmoi apply` on a running box is idempotent and never silently bumps every tool to whatever happens to be latest that day. This matters because:
10	
11	- **Predictability** — rerunning apply after editing one role file shouldn't ripple-upgrade unrelated tools.
12	- **Offline / flaky network** — install-only can be satisfied by what's already on disk; `--upgrade` workflows always hit the network.
13	- **Review friction** — you *want* to see "chezmoi says 10 casks would move; proceed?" as a separate decision from "apply my dotfile changes".
14	
15	The explicit upgrade path lives in [`scripts/upgrade_tools.sh`](../../scripts/upgrade_tools.sh), exposed via `just upgrade-*` recipes in [`justfile`](../../justfile). It is the **only** thing that intentionally moves tools forward on this repo's flow.
16	
17	Two side-effects worth knowing about:
18	
19	- `.chezmoiexternal.toml.tmpl` entries have `refreshPeriod = "168h"` — chezmoi itself will re-fetch those weekly on apply. That's a bounded "nudge", not an upgrade mechanism for installed binaries.
20	- Homebrew casks that carry a `homebrew_cask` entry with `state: present` freeze to that version until a Brewfile hash change forces a re-bundle with `--no-upgrade`. Still install-only; `upgrade-brew` is what actually bumps them.
21	
22	## Entry points
23	
24	```bash
25	just upgrade-all          # externals → brew → mise → uv → npm → cargo → go → dotnet → gem → flatpak → warp → agents → plugins
26	just upgrade-dry-run      # same, but commands are printed, not executed
27	just upgrade-<category>   # run one category in isolation
28	```
29	
30	Or use the script directly when you want the flags:
31	
32	```bash
33	./scripts/upgrade_tools.sh                           # same as 'all'
34	./scripts/upgrade_tools.sh brew uv                   # two categories
35	./scripts/upgrade_tools.sh --only brew,mise          # same, via --only
36	./scripts/upgrade_tools.sh --skip agents,plugins     # all, minus those
37	./scripts/upgrade_tools.sh --dry-run all             # preview
38	./scripts/upgrade_tools.sh --help
39	```
40

## Existing build and install convention

### Makefile

`/Users/david/Worktrees/dev-cli/feat-completion-and-brew/Makefile` is the only packaging-oriented build file.

Relevant variables and targets:

- `BINARY := dev`
- `PREFIX ?= $(HOME)/.local`
- `VERSION := $(shell git describe --tags --always --dirty ... || echo dev)`
- `LDFLAGS := -s -w -X github.com/daviddwlee84/dev-cli/internal/cli.Version=$(VERSION)`
- `build` produces a root-level `./dev` from `./cmd/dev`.

Consequently, a Homebrew formula could not simply reuse `make install` without also triggering user-home writes or sandbox-local writes. The standalone `build` target is separable, however.

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# bootstrap.sh — curl|sh entry for daviddwlee84/dotfiles.
3	#
4	#   curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daviddwlee84/dotfiles/main/bootstrap.sh | bash
5	#
6	# What it does, in order:
7	#   1. Installs `uv` (Astral's Python runtime/tool manager) if missing.
8	#   1b. Ensures a non-snap `~/.local/bin/chezmoi` exists and is first on PATH
9	#      (the snap build has a stdin/stdout `permission denied` bug that breaks
10	#      this repo's modify_/run_ scripts), so the TUI resolves the good binary.
11	#   2. Attaches /dev/tty as the FINAL `exec uv run`'s stdin so questionary
12	#      prompts work even though THIS script's own stdin is the curl pipe.
13	#      We must NOT do `exec </dev/tty` mid-script — that would repoint
14	#      bash's own script reader at /dev/tty and hang on the next line
15	#      (bash reads the script body from fd 0 in `curl | bash` mode, and
16	#      its read behaviour is "undefined" enough to bite on fresh users).
17	#      See: pitfalls/bootstrap-curl-bash-hangs-after-reattaching-tty.md.
18	#   3. Fetches + runs scripts/init/dotfiles_init.py from the pinned ref via
19	#      `uv run --script <url>` — this downloads the script, resolves its
20	#      PEP 723 inline deps into an ephemeral venv, and runs it. No global
21	#      install, no pyproject.toml to maintain.
22	#
23	# Notes:
24	#   - This script is kept in .chezmoiignore.tmpl so `chezmoi apply` does NOT
25	#     deploy it to $HOME/bootstrap.sh.
26	#   - Behind GFW: github.com / raw.githubusercontent.com may be blocked.
27	#     Set DOTFILES_RAW_URL / DOTFILES_REF to a mirror (e.g. ghproxy.com).
28	#     See docs/this_repo/bootstrap.md → "Behind GFW / proxy".
29	#   - Pass extra args through to dotfiles_init (e.g. `| bash -s -- doctor`).
30	#
31	# Verbose mode (recommended for slow networks / first-time runs):
32	#   curl -fsSL .../bootstrap.sh | DOTFILES_BOOTSTRAP_VERBOSE=1 bash
33	#   Sets `set -x`, makes uv print download/resolve progress (`--verbose`),
34	#   and timestamps every stage so you can see where it's stuck.
35	
36	set -euo pipefail
37	
38	DOTFILES_RAW_URL="${DOTFILES_RAW_URL:-https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daviddwlee84/dotfiles}"
39	DOTFILES_REF="${DOTFILES_REF:-main}"
40	SCRIPT_URL="${DOTFILES_RAW_URL}/${DOTFILES_REF}/scripts/init/dotfiles_init.py"
41	VERBOSE="${DOTFILES_BOOTSTRAP_VERBOSE:-0}"
42	
43	log() {
44	    # Timestamped log line so you can spot which stage is slow.
45	    printf '[bootstrap %s] %s\n' "$(date +%H:%M:%S)" "$*" >&2
46	}
47	
48	if [ "$VERBOSE" = "1" ]; then
49	    set -x
50	    UV_RUN_FLAGS=(--verbose)
51	else
52	    UV_RUN_FLAGS=()
53	fi
54	
55	log "starting (ref=${DOTFILES_REF}, raw=${DOTFILES_RAW_URL})"
56	log "PATH=${PATH}"
57	log "TTY: stdin=$([ -t 0 ] && echo yes || echo no), /dev/tty=$([ -r /dev/tty ] && echo readable || echo no)"
58	
59	# --- 1. ensure uv ------------------------------------------------------------
60	if ! command -v uv >/dev/null 2>&1; then
61	    log "uv not found — installing from https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh"
62	    log "(if this hangs >30s, you're likely behind GFW; see docs/this_repo/bootstrap.md)"
63	    curl -fsSL https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
64	    # uv's installer writes to ~/.local/bin by default; add to PATH for this shell.
65	    export PATH="${HOME}/.local/bin:${PATH}"
66	    log "uv installed: $(command -v uv || echo MISSING)"
67	else
68	    log "uv already present: $(command -v uv) ($(uv --version 2>/dev/null || echo unknown))"
69	fi
70	
71	# --- 1b. ensure a non-snap chezmoi on PATH ----------------------------------
72	# The TUI resolves chezmoi via PATH. The snap build has a long-standing
73	# stdin/stdout `permission denied` bug that breaks this repo's modify_/run_
74	# scripts, and is not the install the README documents. So if chezmoi is
75	# missing OR the one found is under /snap, install the canonical binary to
76	# ~/.local/bin; then put ~/.local/bin first on PATH so it always wins.
77	CHEZMOI_FOUND="$(command -v chezmoi 2>/dev/null || true)"
78	NEED_CHEZMOI=0
79	if [ -z "$CHEZMOI_FOUND" ]; then
80	    NEED_CHEZMOI=1
81	    log "chezmoi not found — installing to ~/.local/bin via get.chezmoi.io"
82	elif [ "${CHEZMOI_FOUND#/snap/}" != "$CHEZMOI_FOUND" ]; then
83	    NEED_CHEZMOI=1
84	    log "found snap chezmoi at ${CHEZMOI_FOUND} (stdin/stdout bug) — installing canonical to ~/.local/bin"
85	fi
86	if [ "$NEED_CHEZMOI" = "1" ] && [ ! -x "${HOME}/.local/bin/chezmoi" ]; then
87	    mkdir -p "${HOME}/.local/bin"
88	    if ! (curl -fsLS --retry 3 --retry-delay 5 get.chezmoi.io/lb | BINDIR="${HOME}/.local/bin" sh); then
89	        log "chezmoi install via get.chezmoi.io failed; the TUI will offer to install it"
90	    fi
91	fi
92	# Keep ~/.local/bin first so the canonical chezmoi (and uv-installed tools)
93	# always win over any /snap or system copy.
94	export PATH="${HOME}/.local/bin:${PATH}"
95	log "chezmoi resolved: $(command -v chezmoi || echo MISSING)"
96	
97	# --- 2. decide whether to feed /dev/tty to the final exec --------------------
98	# `[ -t 0 ]` is false when stdin is the pipe; questionary needs a real TTY.
99	# We CANNOT `exec </dev/tty` here — that repoints bash's own fd 0, which
100	# is also where bash reads the rest of THIS script from in `curl | bash`
101	# mode. The next line would then block on /dev/tty waiting for keyboard
102	# input that never comes. Instead we attach /dev/tty as the *child*'s
103	# stdin on the final exec, leaving bash's own fd 0 on the curl pipe.
104	NEED_TTY_REDIRECT=0
105	if [ ! -t 0 ] && [ -r /dev/tty ]; then
106	    log "stdin is a pipe — will attach /dev/tty as uv run's stdin (not bash's)"
107	    NEED_TTY_REDIRECT=1
108	fi
109	
110	# --- 3. run ------------------------------------------------------------------
111	log "fetching + running ${SCRIPT_URL}"
112	log "(first run resolves PEP 723 deps: questionary, rich, tyro — may take 30s-3min on slow networks)"
113	log "(set DOTFILES_BOOTSTRAP_VERBOSE=1 to see uv resolver progress)"
114	if [ "$NEED_TTY_REDIRECT" = "1" ]; then
115	    exec uv run "${UV_RUN_FLAGS[@]}" --script "$SCRIPT_URL" "$@" </dev/tty
116	else
117	    exec uv run "${UV_RUN_FLAGS[@]}" --script "$SCRIPT_URL" "$@"
118	fi
119
```
